threat_model.crown_jewel: personal photos, videos and documents inside the single .cvault file — intimate personal data
adversaries: device thief with the PC or a copy of the .cvault file
shared-household user with OS access to the same profile
casual recipient of the shared EXE or a copied vault file
supply-chain compromise of the Electron binary or a build dependency

findings.title: Renderer-exposed IPC can read, write, and overwrite arbitrary file paths
findings.issue: The preload bridge exposes vault:readFile, vault:writeFile, vault:writeFileAtomic, vault:copyFile, vault:reveal, vault:exists and vault:isDir, and main accepts the renderer-supplied path verbatim with no validation or allowlist. Every path this app legitimately uses originates from main's own dialogs (folder picker, vault picker, save dialogs) or from the remembered vault path — so the renderer never needs arbitrary paths. If any future bug gives an attacker script execution in the renderer (there is no such sink today), the blast radius is full read/write/overwrite of every file the user can access — including replacing vault files or writing executables. This is the standard Electron 'treat every renderer as compromised' hardening gap.
findings.fixed: In main, keep a trusted-paths set populated only from the dialog results (pickFolder, pickVaultFile, saveCopyAs, saveFileAs) and the remembered vault path. Every file IPC handler validates its path against that set (or a descendant of a picked folder) before touching the filesystem; anything else returns an error. The renderer keeps its current API — it never supplies a path main didn't mint.
findings.why_works: A compromised renderer can only reach files the user explicitly picked through a system dialog, so script injection can no longer turn into arbitrary disk access.
findings.poc: Renderer compromise (not reachable today — see chains) → window.vaultAPI.writeFile('C:/Users/HP/Documents/evil.js', bytes) → arbitrary file written with the user's privileges.
findings.resolution: Trusted-path gate implemented in main.js — all 9 file IPC handlers (writeFile/readFile/writeFileAtomic/copyFile/reveal/isDir/exists + the two save dialogs) now validate against dialog-minted paths (vaultPath, lastCopyDst, lastExportDst) before touching the filesystem. Re-checked statically against current main.js (handlers at lines ~195-246): writeFile requires lastExportDst, readFile/writeFileAtomic/reveal/exists require the vault file, copyFile requires vault→backup-dst, isDir requires the vault folder. A compromised renderer can only reach files the user explicitly picked — CHAIN-1 blast radius closed.

findings.title: CSP is strict on scripts but missing the hardening directives
findings.issue: script-src 'self' with no unsafe-eval is the important part and it is right. The gaps are the supporting directives: no object-src 'none' (Flash/plugin fallback), no base-uri 'none' (base-tag injection), no form-action 'self', no frame-ancestors (the app can be framed/clickjacked), and style-src carries 'unsafe-inline' only to support static inline style="..." attributes in the HTML. img-src includes data: which nothing uses.
findings.vulnerable: default-src 'self'; img-src 'self' blob: data:; media-src 'self' blob:; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; script-src 'self'
findings.fixed: default-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; form-action 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'; object-src 'none'; img-src 'self' blob:; media-src 'self' blob:; style-src 'self'; script-src 'self' — and move the ~10 static inline style="..." attributes in index.html into classes so style-src can drop 'unsafe-inline' entirely (the app already sets all dynamic styles via CSSOM, which CSP never blocks).
findings.why_works: Each added directive kills a class of injection/UI-redress attack — a future XSS bug would have no base-tag, plugin, form or frame redirect to amplify it, and style injection cannot smuggle a background:url() exfil.
findings.poc: None today — no script sink exists. The directives are defense-in-depth for the next bug.
findings.resolution: Hardened CSP shipped — src/index.html meta now carries default-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; form-action 'none'; object-src 'none'; img-src 'self' blob:; media-src 'self' blob:; style-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; font-src 'self' with zero inline style attributes (grep style" = 0), and frame-ancestors 'none' is delivered as a real response header in main.js's CSP_HEADER (the only place it works). App boots and renders all screens with no CSP violations.

findings.title: Protocol handler path check uses a string prefix, not a path boundary
findings.issue: filePath.startsWith(path.join(__dirname, 'src')) would also accept a sibling directory whose name begins with 'src' (e.g. src-evil). No such sibling exists today and URL normalization already collapses '..' segments, so nothing is exploitable now — but the guard is one renamable folder away from a real traversal.
findings.fixed:
const srcRoot = path.join(__dirname, 'src');
if (filePath !== srcRoot && !filePath.startsWith(srcRoot + path.sep)) {
findings.why_works: A path-boundary check cannot match sibling prefixes, so the guard survives folder renames.
findings.poc: None today (no sibling src* directory, and URL dot-segments are normalized before the handler runs).
findings.resolution: Path-boundary check applied in main.js protocol handler — now `filePath !== srcRoot && !filePath.startsWith(srcRoot + path.sep)`, so a sibling directory whose name merely begins with 'src' can never pass the guard.

findings.title: Vault file path is remembered in localStorage
findings.issue: pcvault.lastPath stores the absolute path of the vault file. That reveals to anyone with profile/OS access that a vault exists, where it lives, and its filename. No vault content or key material is stored — the vault file itself stays encrypted at rest.
findings.fixed: Acceptable as-is for the stated single-user model. Optional hardening: store only a boolean 'vault exists' hint and resolve the path fresh from the file picker on each launch.
findings.why_works: Removing the path removes the only non-encrypted trace of the vault's existence.
findings.resolution: The renderer no longer keeps the vault path — pcvault.lastPath removed from renderer.js entirely (const + the setItem/removeItem/getItem call sites in tryLoad, handleCreate and boot). Main's userData settings.json is now the single source: new vault:getLastPath / vault:forgetPath IPC return and clear main's own remembered state (no renderer-supplied path moves across the bridge), and boot auto-loads from it exactly as before. No plaintext trace of the vault's location remains in the renderer's storage.

findings.title: Videos and documents keep their original metadata (only photos are EXIF-stripped)
findings.issue: Photos are re-encoded through a canvas so GPS/EXIF never lands in the vault. Videos and docs are stored byte-for-byte, so GPS/author metadata they carry is preserved — encrypted at rest (safe), but an exported or shared copy carries the original metadata. Documented in HANDOFF.md as a known limit.
findings.vulnerable:
const bytes = new Uint8Array(await file.arrayBuffer());
const kind = mime.startsWith('video/') ? 'video' : 'doc';
findings.fixed: Document the tradeoff (already done in HANDOFF.md) or add an optional 'strip metadata on import' pass for videos via ffmpeg-style transcoding — a larger feature, not a security fix.
findings.why_works: Metadata stripping only matters at export/sharing time; at rest it is already encrypted.

findings.title: Tamper self-check decrypts full photos and drops the plaintext without wiping
findings.issue: tamperSample decrypts up to 3 records per unlock — photos at FULL resolution — just to prove the bytes are authentic, then discards the decrypted plaintext without vaultWipeRaw. That is a per-unlock spike of up to ~3 full-res decrypted photos lingering in memory until GC, and it breaks the module's own wipe discipline (every other decBytes caller wipes in a finally). No confidentiality impact (the bytes never leave the process), but the fix is one line.
findings.vulnerable: if (rec.kind === 'photo' && rec.photo) await decBytes(itemKey, rec.photoIv, rec.photo);
findings.fixed: const plain = await decBytes(itemKey, rec.photoIv, rec.photo); vaultWipeRaw(plain);
findings.why_works: The sampled plaintext is zeroed the moment the authenticity check passes, so no decrypted photo bytes linger after unlock.
findings.poc: None — memory-hygiene gap only, no attacker control.
findings.resolution: vaultWipeRaw(plain) added right after the sampled photo decrypt in tamperSample (src/vault-crypto.mjs) — the sampled plaintext is zeroed immediately instead of lingering until GC. Verified in current source.

findings.title: Failed atomic writes leave orphaned .tmp-* files next to the vault
findings.issue: writeFileAtomic writes to `${filePath}.tmp-${process.pid}-${Date.now()}` and renames. If the rename fails (vault file locked by another process, antivirus, disk full), the temp file stays behind. It holds the encrypted vault bytes (no plaintext leak), but orphans accumulate in the vault folder and each is a full copy of the vault — disk usage, not exposure.
findings.fixed: Wrap the rename in try/catch and unlink the tmp file on failure before rethrowing.
findings.why_works: A failed save leaves no copy of the vault behind — only the intact original remains.
findings.poc: None — requires a failing rename (lock/disk-full), and the orphan is encrypted.
findings.resolution: writeFileAtomic now wraps the rename in try/catch and unlinks the .tmp-* file on failure before rethrowing (main.js). Verified in current source.

findings.title: Dev server sends no security headers (CSP header, frame-ancestors, nosniff)
findings.issue: The dev server responds with only content-type. The page's meta CSP still enforces script/img/style policy, but frame-ancestors only works as a real header and nosniff is absent, so a browser-served copy of the page can be framed and its responses can be sniffed. Impact is minimal in practice: the page is inert without the Electron preload bridge (boot fails at vaultAPI.getLastPath — observed live), it binds 127.0.0.1, and it is a dev tool, not the shipped product.
findings.fixed: Add the same CSP_HEADER (with frame-ancestors 'none') and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff to every dev response.
findings.why_works: The browser-served copy then matches the Electron shell's framing and sniffing protections.
findings.poc: Observed live: curl -I http://127.0.0.1:8779/ → only content-type returned. No frame-ancestors on any response.
findings.resolution: server.mjs now sends SECURITY_HEADERS (full hardened CSP incl. frame-ancestors 'none' + X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff) on every dev response. Verified in current source.

findings.title: parseVault has no record-count cap (hostile .cvault can spike CPU/RAM at open and unlock)
findings.issue: parseVault loops records until the buffer ends with no count bound, and tamperSample then sorts ALL records and decrypts a sample on unlock. A crafted .cvault with millions of small records spikes CPU/memory at open and again at unlock. Delivery is realistic under the threat model ('a copied vault file' can be shared with the user), but the file is always user-picked and the result is a local DoS of the app, never code execution. Same class as SEC-006's accepted design limit.
findings.fixed: Optional: cap records (e.g. 100k) and total item bytes before parsing, and reject the file with a clear message.
findings.why_works: A bound converts a hostile-file memory spike into a clean rejection.
findings.poc: None built — static reasoning only; a generated 200k-record file would demonstrate the spike.
findings.resolution: parseVault now enforces MAX_RECORDS = 100000 and returns null (clean rejection) once the cap is hit (src/container.mjs), covered by the container test suite. Verified in current source.

findings.title: Whole files are buffered in memory (import and parse)
findings.issue: handleFiles reads each dropped file fully into RAM (file.arrayBuffer()) and parseVault slurps the entire .cvault file before parsing. A multi-GB video or a huge vault spikes memory. For a single-user personal vault this is a design limit, not a reachable attack — the only person who can feed it oversized input already has the file.
findings.fixed: Optional: add a friendly size warning above ~2 GB per file, and document the limit. Streaming encryption would be the real fix but is a large change.
findings.why_works: A warning converts a silent memory spike into an informed user decision.
findings.resolution: Import size guard added in renderer.js handleFiles — MAX_IMPORT_BYTES = 2 * 1024**3; files over ~2 GB are skipped with a clear toast ("N skipped — over 2 GB (too big to encrypt safely)") instead of being buffered fully into memory. Limit documented in HANDOFF.md. The vault-file parse path remains a documented design limit for personal scale.

If a future code change ever introduces a renderer XSS sink (the audit found zero: all innerHTML uses app-generated BIP39 words or internal object URLs, script-src is 'self' with no unsafe-eval), SEC-001 turns it into full read/write/overwrite of the user's disk.
